topline: Four stories today: an EU joint team heads to the US-brokered Ukraine–Russia talks in Abu Dhabi, Friedrich Merz ties Germany's backing for the next EU budget to all member states funding Ukraine, France blames Iran's Revolutionary Guards for October's cyberattack on supermarket fridges, and Hungarian police detain Viktor Orbán's brother in a people-smuggling probe.

stories.title: EU sends joint team to Abu Dhabi as US-brokered Ukraine–Russia talks resume after nine months
stories.summary: Ukrainian, Russian and US delegations meet in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November for the first round of US-mediated talks since February. The European Commission and European Council are sending a joint team of senior officials, led by Ursula von der Leyen's chief of cabinet Bjoern Seibert and António Costa's foreign-policy adviser Anna-Maria Boura, alongside officials from France, Germany, the UK and NATO. Their exact role is unclear: they may brief and debrief the delegations on the sidelines or join an expanded format, and Brussels has signalled it is willing to meet the Russian side directly. The Kremlin said on Monday the talks would not include Europeans, while Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov said European representatives would be present.
stories.why: Europe has struggled to secure a voice in negotiations that could reshape its own security order, and Giorgia Meloni's complaint about a 'plurality of representatives' is on the agenda of EU leaders' informal meeting in Dublin on 13 November.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage is sceptical that the round will achieve much, leading with analysts who expect no breakthrough on territory or security guarantees. It stresses that Russia still occupies about a fifth of Ukraine and that Donald Trump has pressed Kyiv to cede land, and treats Europe's place at the table as uncertain and contested by Moscow.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Explainer built around analysts who expect no tangible progress; flags the Kremlin's denial of any European role.

outlets.name: CNN
outlets.note: Preview asking what is different about this round after a nine-month pause.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage leads with Paris insisting Europeans will be represented, and stresses the confusion in Brussels over who actually speaks for the bloc. It foregrounds Meloni's demand for a single European voice and the risk of Europe being sidelined, and folds in French attacks on Jean-Luc Mélenchon's stance on Donbas.

outlets.name: Brussels Signal
outlets.note: Leads with Jean-Noël Barrot's reassurances while highlighting contradictory reports on whether the EU would attend.

stories.differ: The left asks whether the talks can succeed at all given Russian demands; the right focuses on whether Europe is organised enough to be heard in them.

stories.title: Merz links Germany's support for next EU budget to all members funding Ukraine
stories.summary: In a letter to European Council President António Costa, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz asked EU leaders to make Ukraine's 2027 financing gap a priority, saying support for Kyiv is a responsibility shared by all member states. Ukraine needs about €70bn next year, of which roughly €45bn is expected to come from the EU, with the source of the money still unresolved. The Financial Times reported that Merz is prepared to block the 2028–2034 long-term budget until every member contributes; Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Bulgaria have signalled they will not. Separately, Parliament and Council negotiators meet today to try to settle the 2027 annual budget, where funding for NextGenerationEU repayments and the Ukraine loan is the main dispute.
stories.why: Tying Ukraine aid to the seven-year budget gives Berlin leverage over holdout states but risks deadlocking negotiations that EU leaders take up in Dublin on 13 November and at a budget summit later this month.

left.angle: Centre-left German coverage presents the move as an ultimatum and walks through Berlin's arguments without endorsing them. It adds context that complicates the burden-sharing claim, citing Kiel Institute figures showing several smaller states give far more per head than Germany.

outlets.name: Berliner Zeitung
outlets.note: Explains the 'ultimatum' and sets Germany's per-capita aid against Denmark's and Sweden's.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage leads with the blunt formula of no money for Kyiv, no EU budget, and casts the four holdout states as net recipients of EU funds refusing to share the cost. It stresses the burden on European taxpayers and treats Merz's hard line as justified pressure.

outlets.name: NIUS
outlets.note: Tabloid-style framing of an 'ultimatum to Brussels'; highlights that the holdouts receive more from the budget than they pay in.

stories.differ: The left-leaning piece questions how fair Germany's burden-sharing complaint really is; the right-leaning piece takes it as given and targets the states that refuse to pay.

stories.title: France blames Iran's Revolutionary Guards for cyberattack on supermarket fridges and seeks EU sanctions
stories.summary: French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said a unit linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the overnight attack of 11–12 October that remotely disrupted refrigeration at more than 700 French stores, including Carrefour, Monoprix and Intermarché outlets. The Paris prosecutor has opened a judicial investigation and requested arrest warrants for the head of the 'Shahid Kaveh' cyber unit and two deputies. France is summoning Iran's ambassador and will push for sanctions at EU level; foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said ministers would discuss attacks across Europe at the 16 November Foreign Affairs Council. Paris puts losses at tens of millions of euros.
stories.why: It is a rare formal attribution of a disruptive civilian-infrastructure cyberattack to a state actor by an EU government, and tests whether the bloc will follow with joint sanctions; MEPs debate critical-infrastructure cyber resilience on Wednesday.

left.angle: Left-leaning outlets report the attribution largely as breaking news, leading with the IRGC link and France's diplomatic response. Al Jazeera's coverage is brief and France-focused, and does not dwell on Iran's wider record or the security implications for Europe.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Short breaking report on the accusation, the summons and the requested arrest warrants.

outlets.name: The Guardian
outlets.note: Headline puts the Revolutionary Guards' alleged role up front.

right.angle: Right-leaning French coverage frames the story as an intelligence finding about the Iranian regime, stressing the unprecedented scale and aggression of the attack. It casts it as a hostile act against France and places it alongside earlier Iranian operations against French targets.

outlets.name: Le Figaro
outlets.note: Exclusive angle: French services 'identify the hand of Iran'; leads with intelligence attribution.

outlets.name: CNews
outlets.note: Reports France holding Iran 'responsible' for the attacks.

stories.differ: Left-leaning outlets treat it mainly as a diplomatic accusation still under investigation; right-leaning French outlets present it as a confirmed act of hostility by Tehran.

stories.title: Hungarian police detain Viktor Orbán's brother in people-smuggling and influence-peddling probe
stories.summary: Hungary's National Bureau of Investigation and the new anti-corruption authority NVVH detained four people on Monday in raids in Budapest and Pest County over the alleged smuggling of more than 100 Vietnamese workers into Hungary using visas obtained through diplomatic missions in 2024. Police did not name the suspects, but Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Hungarian media identified former prime minister Viktor Orbán's younger brother, Áron Orbán, among them; the first report came from a site owned by Magyar's own brother. Many of the migrants are believed to have moved on to other EU countries. Viktor Orbán called the case a political witch hunt and said he, not his brother, was the real target.
stories.why: It is the most prominent case yet in the new government's drive against Orbán-era corruption, and touches Schengen visa integrity across the EU, with Europol supporting the operation.

left.angle: Left-leaning and liberal coverage leads with the raids and the wider anti-corruption sweep, linking the case to earlier reporting on a visa scheme around Áron Orbán's businesses. It is careful that police have not confirmed his identity, but presents Orbán's persecution claim as a defensive reaction rather than the core of the story.

outlets.note: Hungarian independent site; hedged on identity but details the alleged visa and university-course scheme.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Notes the brother's businesses grew during Orbán's 16 years in power, and that the scoop came from the PM's brother's site.

right.angle: We could not find a dedicated take from the right-leaning outlets on our list by publication time. The conservative framing so far comes mainly from Viktor Orbán himself, who presents the arrest as political persecution designed to divert attention and eliminate opponents.

stories.differ: Coverage so far centres on the investigation itself; the competing frame of a politically motivated 'witch hunt' is being carried by Orbán's own statements rather than by right-leaning outlets.

right.title: Europe is trying to patch migration with duct tape
